title: Universal Still Plans Overseas Release for Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Documentary Despite Mogul’s Legal Threats
description:
Sep 17, 2026 6:27pm PT	
	

	
		Universal Still Plans Overseas Release for Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Documentary Despite Mogul’s Legal Threa
body:
Sep 17, 2026 6:27pm PT	
	

	
		Universal Still Plans Overseas Release for Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Documentary Despite Mogul’s Legal Threats
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Courtesy of Venice Film Festival
	

		
	
				
	Contrary to a recent report, Universal is moving forward as planned with the international release of Alex Gibney‘s Elon Musk documentary “Musk,” sources familiar with the project told Variety.

	Though a release date has not yet been set for the overseas rollout, that’s not unusual for a film like “Musk,” a nearly 4-hour long documentary that’s being released theatrically in North American on Oct. 9 by the indie distrib Bleecker Street.
	

	Despite recent legal threats from Musk over the documentary’s content, Universal has always been enthusiastic about releasing the film internationally, the sources added. “Musk” is set to stream on HBO in the first quarter of 2027.


	After the documentary premiered at the Venice Film Festival, the tech mogul began posting comments on X, calling the doc “a hit piece,” though it was not clear whether he had seen the film. 

	Musk asserted that Gibney had “just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me (but still have an axe to grind).” Among the interviews featured in Gibney’s film is one with Ashley St. Clair, a MAGA influencer who had a child with Musk. The documentary portrays a text exchange between the two about the 2024 presidential election.

	Musk’s attorney Alex Spiro threatened to file a defamation lawsuit before the film’s release in October, pointing to Musk’s texts with St. Clair.

	Variety critic Owen Gleiberman wrote in his review of “Musk” in Venice, “Once you start piecing together Musk’s scandals and cut corners and slipshod management, you see that he’s a creator of mirages who promises more than he delivers … Musk, as the documentary makes clear, is a genuine if flawed technocratic visionary, a messianic opportunist, and something of a crackpot,” Universal and Gibney had no comment.


	
		More from Variety

title: Alfonso Cuaron to Make First Korea Visit at Busan as Festival Also Spotlights European Women+ Filmmakers
description: The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has announced the first-ever Korea visit by Alfonso Cuarón, alongside a dedicated spotlight on nin
body:
The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has announced the first-ever Korea visit by Alfonso Cuarón, alongside a dedicated spotlight on nine films from European women and genderqueer filmmakers.

	Cuarón, who has won the Academy Award for best director twice, for “Gravity” (2013) and “Roma” (2018), also holds the Venice Film Festival’s best screenplay prize for “Y Tu Mamá También” (2001) and a Golden Lion for “Roma.” He first caught Hollywood’s attention with “Y Tu Mamá También,” a portrait of youth and desire, before taking “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban” (2004) in a moodier, more personal visual direction than the series had gone before, and later used extended long takes in “Children of Men” (2007) to pull audiences directly into a world at war. He is expected to appear at BIFF’s opening ceremony and will sit down for an extended conversation with festivalgoers about the camera language and instincts behind his films. An Imax screening of “Gravity,” co-written with his son, filmmaker Jonás Cuarón, will also be at the festival.
	

	Jonás Cuarón’s latest feature, “Campeón Gabacho,” will have its Asian premiere in the World Cinema section, followed by a post-screening Q&A. Since writing on “Gravity,” the younger Cuarón has built his own filmography with “Desierto” (2015) and “Chupa” (2023). “Campeón Gabacho,” starring Juan Daniel García Treviño, Leslie Grace, Rubén Blades, Eddie Marsan, Rosario Dawson and Cheech Marin, follows a Mexican immigrant building a life in the United States, and was produced by Jonás Cuarón alongside his father and Gabriela Rodriguez under their Esperanto Filmoj banner, with Nicolás Celis also producing.
	

	Elsewhere at the festival, BIFF is showcasing “Europe! Voices of Women+ in Film,” a program run with the European Film Promotion (EFP), spotlighting nine officially selected films through targeted promotion and industry networking. The lineup spans period drama, documentary and contemporary narrative work built around questions of freedom, memory and family, with four of the nine as feature debuts. May el-Toukhy‘s “Woman Unknown,” winner of the Golden Lion at Venice, anchors the group; el-Toukhy became the first Danish woman filmmaker to take that prize, while Mathilde Arcel won the Volpi Cup for best actress in the same film. Also included are Marine Atlan’s debut “La Gradiva,” Pegah Ahangarani’s “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime,” winner of the Un Certain Regard Prize at Cannes, Margherita Ferrari’s debut “Föa – Once Upon a Future,” Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming,” Marie Kreutzer’s “Gentle Monster,” Shahrbanoo Sadat’s “No Good Men” and Sarah Arnold’s debut “Too Many Beasts.” Judith Godrèche’s “A Girl’s Story,” part of this year’s gala presentations, joins Angela Schanelec’s “My Wife Cries,” Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak’s “Birds of War,” Jacqueline Lentzou’s “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra,” winner of the Horizons Award for Best Director at Venice, and Konstantina Kotzamani’s “Titanic Ocean” among the additional selections.

	Five directors from the program, el-Toukhy, Godrèche, Ferrari, Lentzou and Kotzamani, will travel to Busan to present their films. Godrèche will also take part in a Cine Class session, “Women, Rewriting the Screen,” and BIFF and EFP will co-host a Talk-to-Talk panel, “Women Directors: Taking the Scene,” bringing together Ferrari, el-Toukhy and Lentzou alongside Iranian director Marjan Khosravi (“Dreams of the Wild Oaks”), Chinese director Michelle Zhou (“Big Little Things”) and Afghan director Zainab Entezar (“771 Days”).

	BIFF programmer Seo Seunghee said that in reviewing films for this year’s festival, she noticed European women directors becoming more prominent among the strongest titles under consideration, in both volume and quality. “Moreover, the fact that four of the nine invited films are feature debuts is also an indicator of the generational shift taking place in European cinema,” Seo said. “Our ongoing collaboration with EFP has become a reliable channel for discovering and validating outstanding films and filmmakers, and the results are fully reflected in this year’s lineup.”
	

	EFP managing director Irina Ignatiew-Lemke said the “Europe! Voices of Women+ in Film” initiative lets EFP and its member organizations “join forces to give distinctive European voices greater international visibility.” She added, “Busan is an important platform for bringing these filmmakers and their works into dialogue with audiences and industry professionals in Asia. By combining the festival’s selection with EFP’s targeted promotion and networking, we are proud to support underrepresented voices and create opportunities for the next generation of women+ filmmakers.”

	The program runs in collaboration with BIFF, the Sydney Film Festival and Festival do Rio, with support from the Creative Europe – MEDIA Programme of the European Union. This year’s participating national film promotion organizations are Austrian Films, Cinecittà, the Czech Film Center, the Danish Film Institute, German Films and Unifrance, with Cineuropa serving as media partner.

	The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and venues throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13.

title: Nick Kroll Delivers Heartfelt Appeal for Productions to Shoot in L.A.: ‘It Will Bring Life Back’ to the City
description: Nick Kroll said upcoming Netflix comedy series “A Hundred Percent,” which he co-created and stars in, is a “love letter” to Los Angeles — and he exp
body:
Nick Kroll said upcoming Netflix comedy series “A Hundred Percent,” which he co-created and stars in, is a “love letter” to Los Angeles — and he expressed hope that a “thriving” entertainment production community will bring “vitality” to the city.

	The comedian, writer, producer, director and actor was a featured keynote speaker at the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY, held Thursday in L.A.


	Kroll explained why he “needed” to film “A Hundred Percent,” which is expected to debut on Netflix in 2027, in L.A. “It feels like it’s about people who live in Los Angeles. I’ve lived here for almost 20 years,” he said.
	

	He co-created “A Hundred Percent” with his friend Gabe Liedman (creator of “Q-Force” and showrunner of the first season of “PEN15”), and stars in the show alongside Sam Richardson, Jason Mantzoukas and Vanessa Bayer, with Diane Lane joining the cast in a recurring role.

	“We genuinely felt like it was a love letter to the city that we live in. And we really, honestly, have the best crew, had the best people, who were in such a happy mood making a show in Los Angeles,” said Kroll, who was interviewed on stage by Angelique Jackson, senior entertainment writer at Variety. “It was an awesome experience, and I’m so grateful to the city for helping make that happen. I hope it continues to grow because I think all of the doldrums that we’ve all been feeling for so many years will hopefully begin to work itself out.”

	Kroll continued: “The more that we have a thriving, ongoing shooting community here in Los Angeles, it will bring life back. Not only money, but just like it will bring a vitalization, a vitality to the city that I think I have missed from when I moved here, and like the dream of coming to Hollywood and making things and being around people who are making things.”
	

	When the audience responded with a round of applause, Kroll then quipped: “That said, I’m personally moving to Austin to start a podcast network.”

	“A Hundred Percent,” Kroll said, is a “show about the world of thought leaders, self-help gurus, wellness influencers, and much of where they sort of live are on panels like this, in sad ballrooms” — he gestured to the Four Seasons room where he was speaking at the conference — “where you only get pitchers of water, tiny mints, and if you really search, a San Pellegrino, but that’s not what matters.”

	Kroll said his goal with any project is “just trying to first and foremost work with the most talented people I can find.” In the case of “A Hundred Percent,” he said Liedman, the cast and the writers “are the funniest people… It’s just an incredibly talented group.”

	“Just surround yourself with quality people, because assholes — they’re just the worst, you know. So that’s what I would say,” Kroll said. He added, “That’s a pretty profound statement, if Variety wants to lead with that.”

	In addition to his work on “A Hundred Percent,” Kroll is an executive producer of the FX sitcom “Adults,” which follows five 20-something friends living together in Queens, New York (in one of the group’s childhood homes). He has also served as EP and voice actor for several Netflix animated series, including “Mating Season,” “Human Resources” and the Emmy-nominated “Big Mouth.”

	Kroll and “Adults” creators Ben Kronengold and Rebecca Shaw started developing the show several years ago, “and then we cast the next generation of incredibly funny comedic performers, and they fucking killed it.”

	“Adults” comes under Kroll’s long-running first-look deal with FX, a relationship with the network that began more than 15 years ago. He said he loves making fun of FX’s “fearless” tagline but said it’s true that “they are genuinely incredibly innovative in how they launch stuff and how they’re willing to take shots. And in the case of ‘Adults,’ Season 1 found an audience, but it wasn’t as big an audience as everyone wants. And so we shot this prequel episode to give a new way into the show.”

	Through that episode, Kroll explained, “audiences found it, really responded to it, and then were able to understand the show and the characters in a way that they entered into the rest of the season and stuck around.” In Season 2, bucking typical TV trends, the show’s ratings grew by 40% domestically and 100% internationally. “It’s a testament to FX and John Landgraf at the head of it to trust us to build something to keep with something that they know is quality and that’s what it comes down to.”
	

	About creating engaging TV shows, Kroll said, “I really think it’s such incredible competition for people’s attention that you really have to figure out a way to grab them, but also hold them gently, so that they don’t run away. And that’s the hard thing to figure out. That’s the game we’re all in right now.”

	At the beginning of his talk, Kroll riffed on the previous panel about AI in the entertainment industry — in which there was a sentiment expressed that humans will always find a way to keep the tech in check — Kroll commented, “Don’t underestimate the ability of machines to find a way to destroy us as well,” adding, “I say that generally without much alarm.”

title: ‘Tenzing’ Actor Tenzin Dalha Unveiled as Male Lead in Bengali Thriller ‘Chheledhora’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Tenzin Dalha, at the Toronto Film Festival with Jennifer Peedom’s Apple original Film “Tenzing,” has been revealed as the male lead in Bengali-langu
body:
Tenzin Dalha, at the Toronto Film Festival with Jennifer Peedom’s Apple original Film “Tenzing,” has been revealed as the male lead in Bengali-language thriller “Chheledhora,” opposite Swastika Mukherjee. 

	His casting had been withheld when the Indo-American production was first announced earlier this year, with producers naming only Mukherjee at that point.

	“Tenzing,” a gala presentation at TIFF, features Genden Phuntsok as legendary mountaineer Tenzing Norgay, with Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe and Caitríona Balfe also in the cast. A limited theatrical run begins Oct. 9, with global streaming on Apple TV following Oct. 16.
	

	In “Chheledhora,” written and directed by Shieladitya Moulik – whose credits include “Sweater” and “Surjo” – Dalha and Mukherjee anchor a story set off by an act of parental defiance. Mukherjee plays Brishti, a divorced mother who “steals” her own daughter for a birthday outing, only for the child to be genuinely abducted. The discovery then draws a group of deeply flawed adults and their children into an erratic journey through Northeast India, where the youngest characters gradually emerge as the moral compass for the adults around them. Filmed extensively in Arunachal Pradesh’s Ziro Valley, the production combines family drama, thriller elements and dark humor with the cultural texture of India’s Northeast. It is currently in post-production.

	“We made a very conscious decision not to announce Tenzin when we first revealed ‘Chheledhora,'” said Ann Mukherjee, founder of Indo-American production company Sita22 Films. “We knew he had this extraordinary international moment ahead of him with ‘Tenzing,’ and TIFF felt like exactly the right time for audiences to discover another side of him. Tenzin possesses a quiet emotional intelligence and restraint that makes him a fascinating counterpoint to Swastika’s tremendous emotional force. Their chemistry is central to the film.”
	

	Mukherjee described “Chheledhora” as a film that makes both a physical and emotional journey into India’s Northeast. “We want to tell stories that are deeply rooted in India but aren’t constrained by conventional ideas of language, geography or identity,” she said.

	Dalha said it felt “particularly special” to be discussing one project while at the festival for another. “They are completely different films, yet rooted in human grit, empathy, the lengths to which humans are capable of going for people they love,” he said. “What drew me to ‘Chheledhora’ was Shieladitya’s writing. His understanding of humans as imperfect complex beings and looking at life beyond the dichotomy of individuals as good or bad. He wrote these beautiful broken young adult characters making questionable choices for their loved ones.”

	The actor described Mukherjee as “a force of nature in frame and a force of joy on set,” adding that the Arunachal landscape shaped the film’s atmosphere from the outset. “Shooting in Ziro and Arunachal Pradesh provided the perfect backdrop for a thriller, and the weather set the tone right for the ambience,” he said.

	The film is produced by Ann Mukherjee for Sita22 Films, with Jitin Hingorani as co-producer and creative producer, Dhanraj Sawant as executive producer and Priyangi Borthakur as supervising producer. Italian cinematographer Vincenzo Condorelli shot the film.

	“The idea was never to make a Bengali film that simply happens to travel to the Northeast,” said Hingorani, who also heads content and development at Sita22 Films. “The journey changes these characters, and the Northeast becomes part of the film’s emotional language. Pairing Swastika and Tenzin gives us two performers coming from very different cinematic and cultural energies, and that tension is part of what makes the film so exciting. At Sita22, our mandate is to find stories that can be hyper-local and super-global at the same time, and ‘Chheledhora’ embodies that philosophy beautifully.”

title: Battling Misconceptions and Figuring Out Use Cases: Entertainment Leaders Navigate AI’s Place in the Industry
description: In a world where AI is capturing every conversation, a series of experts is trying to figure out what it actually means for the world of entertainme
body:
In a world where AI is capturing every conversation, a series of experts is trying to figure out what it actually means for the world of entertainment.

	“I think the word ‘AI’ is doing too much right now,” says Mira Line, Google’s vice president of technology and society. ”One of the things that we’re doing, especially with the industry, is figuring out, well, what does AI mean in the industry? How do you break it down?”
	

	Lane made her comments alongside several entertainment and tech personalities during the “Entertainment and Media in the Age of AI” panel, one of several AI-focused conversations happening at Variety’s Entertainment and Tech Summit presented by EY. Moderated by Variety business editor Todd Spangler, the conversation saw executives from Netflix (Girish Balakrishnan, the streamer’s senior director, creative innovation), Lionsgate (Kathleen Grace, its chief AI officer), Hasbro (Bertie Thomson, head of its AI-focused studio Sixth Wall), Teads (Annaka Vasquez, senior vice president of sales) and Adobe (Meagan Keane, Pro Video’s head of business strategy) come together to walk through AI’s place in entertainment and the use cases for versions of the technology — once people figure out how to talk about it.


	That comes down to building relationships with creators about how it can be used, including where it fits within the production landscape. Balakrishnan highlighted Netflix’s public framework for how the company uses AI within its production pipeline (on a generative level, for roughly 300 programs), a model he said “builds trust with the creative community” and gives those members ”a pathway to navigate to drive use cases that are meaningful to the creative process.”
	

	The industry is already landing on other frameworks surrounding AI’s place in the industry, such as the Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute-led “Human Generative Workflows” paper published last month. Lane helped develop the paper, which she said breaks down the use cses in ways that can help AI-backed productions reach a still-elusive goal: being copyrightable.

	“We did a whole exercise around tooling and looking at everything from de-noising techniques to fully synthetic characters,” she said. “Let’s start thinking about the vocabulary and breaking it down so it’s not just AI as one big monolithic.”

	Adobe has tried to help distinguish that in its own tools, Keane said, delineating between “assistive,” “corrective“ and “generative” functions. That allows users who’ve found those use cases to prosper, she said. “People don’t even really realize that they’re AI anymore because so much of the conversation has shifted to generative,” she said.

	Some of that trust built between companies and those working in the AI space has offered up another elusive item in the field: intellectual property, including renowned brands and high-profile characters.

	“[Companies] are very careful about how we use those creative assets to maintain the integrity of the brand,” Vasquez said about Teads’ work with ad sales. “We have AI models to build the creative, but for those world’s largest brands, there’s a lot of scrutiny around that. So what I’m looking forward to, and the brands that we partner [with] look forward to, is what are the guardrails in place?”

	Hasbro, through its Sixth Wall work, has worked to implement proprietary guardrails for the ElevenLabs-backed AI replicas of characters it licenses, such as those of Cobra Commander and Optimus Prime. While companies can license those characters for interactive experiences — one hypothetical Thomson offered was a Waymo with the voice of Prime — those can’t be manipulated in the way many unauthorized clips of Hasbro characters have been.

	“If you think about the existence of lots of unauthorized characters out there… they’re not necessarily safe for our brand,” Thomson said. “Whereas working on the authorized AI version of the character means that, for these actors, it has a protective value for them too, and also for us as IP owners.”
	

	Still, each company is still working through public misconceptions surrounding AI, whether the idea models are preparing for humanity’s imminent destruction or the notion that full-fledged blockbusters can be create with a quick prompting of ChatGPT.

	“They don’t understand that, when you’re making really premium movies, TV shows, really engaging stories the way that Lionsgate and others on the stage do, the technology you have to use there is more complex than just prompting. It’s a whole process,” Lane said. “There’s a lot of consideration that goes into everything we make, and in my role, I’m here [saying] here are the tools you could use to make your thing better, bigger, more, and get to the end of the production faster. You choose what’s best for the story, and then, great, you chose the thing that’s best for your story, and it’s better. It’s not necessarily what people think of in pop culture. It’s not like ChatGPT. We just can’t throw something onto that.”

	In the end, each leader said they wanted the technology to help creatives tell better — and more — stories, not feel like they have to adopt the technology for the sake of staying ahead.

	“Filmmakers aren’t asking, ‘Do I want to use AI or not?’ They’re looking to solve meaningful creative problems that they’re faced with on their shows,” Balakrishnan said, citing several Netflix programs that made use of generative AI. “I think those are the opportunities that creators are looking for, and that’s where AI comes specific as an option to be able to solve real creators.”

	It can also, in Grace’s view, help studios find and distribute new stories from creators who’ve utilized AI tools to help bring their visions to life. She cited the worlds of “John Wick” and “The Hunger Games” as examples of work the company has done to sell well-liked IP, and that it wants to have “all kinds of filmmakers we work with.” 

	“Just look at the range of our slate from this year: ‘Housemaid,’ ‘Michael,’ ‘Sunrise [on the Reaping]’,” she said. “Those are all very different filmmakers and different stories. To me, it’s just more creative people, and in some ways, easier to find them because the tools are democratized. Is it going to be an exciting challenge to bring in more talented people who have access to tools? Yes, but I’m interested to see what happens.”

title: With Lucas Museum About to Open, Mellody Hobson Steps Down From LA28 Olympics Board
description: Just days before the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opens to the public, co-founder Mellody Hobson has stepped down from the board of directors of Lo
body:
Just days before the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opens to the public, co-founder Mellody Hobson has stepped down from the board of directors of Los Angeles Olympics organizing committee LA28, Variety has confirmed. 

	Hobson indicated that the demands of overseeing the Lucas Museum, which opens Tuesday after a Friday gala, were too great to continue serving on the board, according to an email reviewed by LAist. Business executive Hobson is co-founder of the museum with her husband George Lucas. 
	

	The 35-person board is led by Casey Wasserman, who was forced to give up his stake of his management company after the Epstein files revealed his messages with Ghislaine Maxwell. 


	An activist group called the Fair Games Coalition has sought to meet with Hobson over their concerns about the Olympics and Paralympics, including housing and workers’ needs. The coalition is also concerned about the games’ effect on the South Los Angeles area that is home to the Lucas Museum.

	“The Fair Games Coalition is deeply disappointed that Mellody Hobson responded to requests to meet with faith leaders, workers and community members calling for living wages, affordable housing, immigrant protections, and Games that benefit all Angelenos by announcing she was resigning from the LA28 Board,” the group said in a statement. 

	“Mellody Hobson could have used her influence on the LA28 Board to stand with our communities, support living wages, and defend immigrant workers. Instead, she chose the easy way out. That is deeply disappointing,” Rev. Gary Williams, Senior Pastor of St. Mark United Methodist Church, a member of the Fair Games Coalition, said in the group’s statement.

title: San Sebastián 2026: ‘Les Mis,’ Los Javis, Brad Pitt, Penélope Cruz and Much More
description:
Ten takes on this year’s San Sebastián Film Festival, which runs Sept. 18-26 at the picturesque Basque Country resort: 

	Brad Pitt, Penelope Cruz,
body:
Ten takes on this year’s San Sebastián Film Festival, which runs Sept. 18-26 at the picturesque Basque Country resort: 

	Brad Pitt, Penelope Cruz, Naomi Watts and More

	Last in San Sebastián way back then with “Inglourious Basterds,” Brad Pitt returns for “Heart of the Beast.” Busiest star of the festival? Penelope Cruz, fresh off a TIFF Special Tribute Award, at San Sebastián with “The Invite,” “Bunker” and “La Bola Negra,” all moreover Oscar contenders, as Awards season conversation spills over into San Sebastián. “Bunker” and “The Beloved” screenings should attract Javier Bardem. Watts receives a prestigious Donostia Award Sept. 19, New German Cinema leading light Werner Herzog picks up his at San Sebastián’s Sept. 18 opening ceremony.
	



	

					James Belmont (Brad Pitt) and Odin in ‘Heart of the Beast’ from Paramount Pictures.
									Scott Garfield
	



	San Sebastián-CAA Media Finance Creative Investors Conference


	From 2022, speakers like Roeg Sutherland, Patrick Wachsberger, Vincent Maraval and Neon’s Sarah Colvin have laid it on the line on how to confront challenges in the U.S. (cost, contracting budgets, unreliable tax breaks) and Europe (most recently, the need to scale), plus more promisingly, an evolution in U.S. theatrical audiences. Speakers this year take in execs from Acme AI & FX, Black Bear International, Media Capital Technologies, Mubi, Neon, Studiocanal and Sumerian Pictures, the Larraín brothers and Rodrigo Teixeira. Topics include the New U.S. Landscape, Europe’s Current Challenges & Opportunities and Vincent Maraval’s Insights from Goodfellas.
	

	Spain Has Never Had It Better

	In 2024, the last year for which figures are available, global streamers poured €2.0 billion ($2.3 billion) into Spain, €0.8 billion ($0.9 billion) into France, €0.7 million ($0.8 billion) into Germany, according to the European Audiovisual Observatory. Spain made 423 features last year, France 228: Cannes Marché du Film Focus report estimates. In TV, Netflix Spain has just shepherded the Mallorca shoot, much in the Mallorquín local language, of “Rafa,” the first non-English language series to score a Primetime Emmy nomination. “Spanish Cinema has never been more powerful, with so many international titles,” says San Sebastián Festival Director José Luis Rebordinos. That power plays out across the whole festival.

	‘La Bola Negra,’ San Sebastian’s Biggest Movie

	One case in point: It’s a mark of synergies struck between festivals that the biggest title at San Sebastián, at least for local audiences, already played at Cannes: the French Festival’s biggest Oscar contender, “La Bola Negra,” a Movistar Plus Original. “We’re being flooded with requests for tickets and we haven’t even announced its screening date, let alone opened sales,” Rebordinos told Variety late August. Launching its first movie slate, SVOD-pay TV Movistar Plus talked about backing event auteur films. In “La Bola Negra,” from Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, it has its biggest yet.

	Spain’s Finest Hour at San Sebastián

	And another: San Sebastián’s Made in Spain, its recent Spanish standouts strand, framed an average 11 films over 2018-22. In 2026, it will showcase 24 including Pedro Almodovar’s “Bitter Christmas” and Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s “The Beloved” (though the both have opened in Spain). Playing out of competition are “After Society,” J.A. Bayona’s follow up to “Society of the Snow,” and Oscar winner Fernando Trueba’s country-hopping “Bajañí.” “Flamenco Sketches,” from double San Sebastián Golden Shell winner Isaki Lacuesta, bows in Zabaltegi.

	Buzz Titles & Discoveries

	There’s big expectation for the world premiere of “Les Miserables,” an epic, but more realistic thriller take on the classic from Fred Cavayé and Studiocanal. Michaël R. Roskam’s fest closer “Le Faux Soir” and series “El Castillo” count among buzz titles. As for new directors, there’s good word on titles from Japan’s Maha Harada (“In My Father’s Room”) in competition and in New Directors pics from Norway’s Marlene Emile Lyngstad (“Cute”), Brit Billy Lumby (Florid”), Kazakh Anna Nurdinova (“Mugalim) and Mexico’s Rodrigo García Saiz (“Morro”). Anybody who hasn’t caught Clara Simón’s sensational “Flamenco” has a chance to do so on Monday, with the director in attendance.
	

	Pablo Larráin, Benjamín Naishat

	“I’m convinced that in 10 years time Rodrigo Sorogoyen and Los Javis will be among the most important directors in the world,” says Rebordinos. Another Spanish-language filmmaker, Chile’s Pablo Larraín, has arguably already made the grade. The director of “Jackie,” “Spencer” and “Maria” has at San Sebastián the world premiere of “My Sad Dead,” a movie format presentation of the Netflix TV series and one of the buzziest of competition contenders. Naishtat segues from Toronto with “Glaxo,” packing a scene-stealing turn by Lali Espósito. “She reminds me of the stars of classic Hollywood studios cinema,” says Rebordinos.



	

					Lali Espósito in ‘Glaxo’
									Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures
	



	One of San Sebastián’s Big Questions

	This July, Movistar Plus, behind “The New Years,” “La Mesías” and “Querer,” announced it will double Spanish original series production from 8 to 16 a year, co-producing or acquiring 10 more. “Movistar Plus is still the foremost home for Spanish creativity. We aim to build even more on that sense of local ambition, but looking for titles with international relevance,” Movistar Plus Contents Director Juan Andrés García Ropero “Bropi” tells Variety. In films, Movistar Plus also co-produced ““Sirāt,” “The Beloved” and “La bola negra.” The industry will be looking for hints at San Sebastián as to Movistar Plus’ movie production roadmap.

	Made in Spain allows critics and distributors to catch up on films they’ve missed, allowing another opportunity for earlier in the year titles, says Rebordinos.

	Basque Cinema’s Newest Generation

	There’s no Basque film in main competition this year, which is quite unusual, down from three titles in 2025. That’s not to say that there aren’t notable Basque films. Igor Legarreta’s “Blind Ants” weighs in as a calling card for Basque Country production standards. There’s good word on “The Last Goodbye,” Koldo Almandoz (“Mouths of Sand”), one of the most distinctive of Basque auteurs, plus Javier Giner’s “This Solitude” in New Directors and Nitya López Saitua’s “Family Drill” in Zinemira, first features from a newer generation of Basque directors whose ranks are fast swelling.

	José Luis Rebordinos’s Swan Song
	

	When Rebordinos appeared on stage this July at Madrid’s Academia de Cine to present San Sebastian’s Spanish titles, the industry-press audience got to its feet to a man and woman to deliver him a standing ovation. Few festival directors have proved so popular. Among his achievements since 2010: Stability, sponsors, a battling candor on hot-button issues, an industry build and the vision to frame and help drive Spain’s emergence as one of Europe’s key film-TV powers. Rebordinos’ Madrid tribute will not be his last. With Maileen Beloki, his successor from Jan. 2027, a member of Rebordinos’ team from 2016, expect evolution not revolution: You don’t tear down one of the loveliest festivals in the world.



	

					José Luis Rebordinos

title: Top Marketers on How Creators, TikTok, Spotify and Pinterest Help Fuel Fandom
description: The era of AI and social media platforms has blown open the marketing playbook for bringing audiences to entertainment and experiences. That was the
body:
The era of AI and social media platforms has blown open the marketing playbook for bringing audiences to entertainment and experiences. That was the sentiment shared by six top marketers who spoke Thursday at Variety‘s Entertainment and Technology Summit in Los Angeles.

	The subject of the creator economy and its impact on selling everything from soap to soap operas was a dominant theme of the day. And it was center stage in the panel with executives from Archrival, TikTok, Spotify, Pinterest, AMC Global Media and Lionsgate, which was moderated by Dea Lawrence, Variety‘s publisher and co-president.
	

	Entertainment marketers once closely guarded their marketing materials and spooned out their campaigns with tactical precision on timing and platforms. Social media and social video in particular require studios and creatives to allow their fans to offer their takes on their favorite properties. It’s particularly prevalent on TikTok, of course.


	“That participatory culture of co-creation is so unique to us, and that’s why [TikTok] participants are very engaged in creating,” said Dawn Yang, global head of entertainment for TikTok. “We have over 12 million TV and film posts that are posted by our users every day now, and that just gives you the perspective how much content there is around just stories that they love and want to share with everyone.”

	Briana McElroy, global head of digital marketing for Lionsgate’s Motion Picture Group, reinforced Yang’s point by sharing her own experience.

	“We actually hire fans to make our TikTok content for Lionsgate brand. If you consume it, you’ll know it — it’s called edits on TikTok,” McElroy said. “That’s wildly popular, and it’s really a lot of kids — 17 year olds, 18 year olds, 15 year olds — it’s their way of expressing their love for a person or a movie or a musician. They create these incredible visual pieces. The temptation is to try to replicate that on our end. But we thought, why do that? If we’re talking about authenticity, the best way to do it is to let the fans themselves do it. So on TikTok, that piece of advertising is incredible.”
	

	Ben Harms, chief growth officer at youth culture marketing agency Archrival, offered a strong point of view on what it takes to win today and in the future. 

	“The brands that are going to win over the next 10 years are the ones that understand how to truly add value into consumers’ lives,” Harms said. He pointed to Spotify as a prime example. “While we have so much data and we’ve optimized and engineered everything, there is this sense that we’ve sort of lost the magic of the world in a lot of ways. And what we find that’s working for brands today is when they’re building ecosystems of experiences and human connection that go far beyond attention and just getting noise out there to really building meaningful connections with consumers.”

	Sara Pollack, global head of consumer marketing for Pinterest, also reinforced that today’s fans often want to craft elaborate tributes and nods to favorite personalities and titles. On the Pinterest platform, fans hunt for inspiration for expressing their love.

	“It’s like they’re coming to Pinterest to figure out how to turn that fandom into real world moments and experiences that they share with others that feel rich and fulfilling,” Pollack said. She cited a recent brand partnership that Pinterest struck with Warner Bros. to promote the theatrical release of “Practical Magic 2.” 

	“We saw that there’s a ton of Gen Z sourcing happening for really like specific things like herbal apothecaries, crystal meanings, tarot readings. This is all really adjacent to the film,” Pollack said. “So for Gen-Zers who maybe didn’t see the first [film], but clearly would be an immediate fan of the second, given what they’re already looking for — that was an opportunity for us to come together and actually build a real world pop-up experience where people could come and get tarot card readings. They could custom make candles. They could figure out how to create their own brew of tea. And that means that from every moment forward, it’s an actual connection to to the film and to Pinterest that goes beyond just an impression or a share or a like.”

	Jenny Haggard, global head of thought leadership at Spotify, added her perspective that marketers too often use “Gen Z” as a broad brush. Spotify has made a point of understanding this cohort with an annual report that studies the consumption habits of the demo defined as ages 14-29 — which is a pretty broad range of life stages, Haggard observed.
	

	“The first mistake we see marketers make is they treat Gen Z as one group,” she said. “I don’t know about you, but I was a very different person from when I was a teeny bopper dancing to NSYNC in my bedroom than when I was 29 and young professional working and living in New York. What we’ve learned is that life stage is a better predictor of behavior than birth year, and so I think we as marketers need to stop doing that.”

	Haggard also made a strong stand that the conventional wisdom that teens and young adults don’t have the patience to watch long-form content.

	“As an industry, it’s now common practice to make ads that are six seconds long,” she said. “I went into our dashboards and found that a third of older Gen Zs on Spotify are streaming 100% of two-hour-long podcast episodes. So what that tells me is that Gen Z isn’t allergic to long-form content; they’re allergic to shitty content. We all know this. James Cameron would be out of a job if people didn’t like long form content. To me, it’s about creating better content. That is our responsibility as marketers.”

	Kim Granito, chief marketing officer for AMC Global Media, echoed Haggard comments that the new world order puts pressure on marketers to be as creative as fans.

	“It’s our job as marketers to make sure that we are creating on ramps for them to find and experience [entertainment] exactly where they want to,” Granito said. “There are fans of ‘The Walking Dead’ has been around for 15 years. There are people that show up for every single spinoff series, but don’t necessarily post about it or do things, and there are other fans that dress up as Negan every year at Comic Con and bring their families and friends along. The passion and love that they have for that IP is the same. It’s expressed differently. So I think it’s our job as marketers to create as broad a pathway and is layered, choose-your-own-adventure journey for them to make it their own.”

	(Pictured: Variety‘s Dea Lawrence, TikTok’s Dawn Yang, Lionsgate’s Briana McElroy, Spotify’s Jenny Haggard, AMC Global Media’s Kim Granito, Archrival’s Ben Harms and Pinterest’s Sara Pollack)

body:
Sep 17, 2026 7:01pm PT	
	

	
		‘The Traitors: New Blood’ EPs Break Down NBC Premiere, Sweetening the Pot for the Faithful and Why the Civilian Cast ‘Played Hard Straight Away’
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Euan Cherry/NBC
	

		
	
				

	SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for the two-hour series premiere of NBC’s “The Traitors: New Blood,” now streaming on Peacock.

	“The Traitors” castle isn’t just for the rich and famous anymore. Peacock’s Emmy-winning franchise has arrived on NBC, with “The Traitors: New Blood,” a new season composed entirely of civilian players in the game of murder, mayhem and more money than ever before.

	In the show’s two-hour series premiere, host Alan Cumming welcomed 22 appropriately bloodthirsty competitors to his Scottish castle and immediately threw them into the deep end of the loch. Because of the show’s international popularity, the players walked into the castle knowing exactly where to go and what to investigate. Feeling right at home with the game is exactly what the creative team wanted.

	“To have a sense of familiarity meant they felt comfortable in their surroundings and they played hard straight away,” executive producer Sam Rees-Jones tells Variety of the premiere.

	At the first roundtable, with a sly tap on the shoulder, Cumming chose Tomica Adams (a pilot from Boston, MA) and Joe Vanella (a funeral director from Wantagh, New York) as his first Traitors of the season. But during their midnight confab in the turret, he informed them a third Traitor was incoming, and that they had to pick the person. In addition to their first murder (RIP faux college basketball coach and real lawyer Kim Daily), the Traitors chose two “accomplices” to audition to become their fellow chaos agent.



	

									Courtesy of Euan Cherry/NBC
	




	Katie Fites (a marketing manager from Jacksonville, Florida, and the youngest player at 23) and Xavier Scruggs (former MLB player turned analyst) got to work scheming and stirring the pot against each other to claw their way to the turret. But the ultimate test came in the second hour when they were directed to deceive the Faithfuls in plain sight by stealing a cleverly titled book on crime and punishment and delivering it to the Traitors. The premiere leaves audiences hanging on whether they manage to smuggle the book out without the Faithful seeing it..

	What is for sure is that the blood of the Faithfuls has already been spilled. In addition to Daily’s murder, a tense first roundtable saw Mississippi realtor Kriste Lewis go for the jugular on San Diego construction manager Madeline Kostopulos over a throwaway comment she believed proved she was one of the cloaked killers. Caught in the crossfire was Kostopulos’ ally and resident eye candy, New York business executive Victor Vollbrechthausen, who took heat for immediately snagging a shield of protection in the first challenge. The pair nearly split the vote evenly.


	Below, “The Traitors: New Blood” executive producers Rosie Franks, Mike Cotton and Rees-Jones go deep on slimming down their hit for broadcast, why they incentivized identifying Traitors for the first time and how including an all-civilian cast makes the game so much more personal.

	
		Being on broadcast means these episodes run for about 41-42 minutes, along with the commercial breaks. That’s very different from the Peacock episodes, which often exceed an hour. How does the time constraint change the storytelling and the rhythm of the show?	

	Mike Cotton: I would say that was one of our biggest challenges. In truth, the game is the game. We call it a game, but there’s always a cycle. It’s a day in the castle. There’s always breakfast, someone gets murdered, there’s the mission, there’s a roundtable, and the Traitors meet in the turret. We haven’t changed that, in terms of how they played the game. But we had to look at different places where we could create cliffhangers, and so we put quite a lot of thought and work into that before we started shooting to make sure that the audiences still got what “The Traitors” was. We always say we’re like a murder mystery, but we treated it a bit like a drama. Where’s a good place for a cliffhanger? We actually put quite a lot of planning in our pre-production to work out those different points that could cliffhanger the episodes. One thing we didn’t want to do is cut it like it’s a drama. We didn’t want to make the episodes faster or fit everything into a short amount of time. We still wanted to breathe and be able to explore the characters, and I feel like we’ve achieved it.



	

									Courtesy of Euan Cherry/NBC
	




	
		You’re at a disadvantage this season where you don’t have the backstory of celebrities to help you prep. In the premiere, we see one of the competitors holding a card that asks their preference to play as a Traitor or Faithful. Is that something you’ve always done, or is that new reconnaissance this season?	

	Sam Rees-Jones: No, that was something new for the civilians. What we loved about this version was Alan inviting these players. He sent out these invitations, so it should feel like these players are actually being invited to this crazy experience in the Highlands of Scotland. And within that invitation was whether they wanted to be a Traitor or a Faithful.

	Rosie Franks: Alan always asks them in the “gold chats” by the fire in the premiere what role they want to play in the game. But this just felt like a really nice throughline from the opening of the raven flying across America, dropping the invitations, and this is like their RSVP.

	Rees-Jones: We pick Traitors only if they want to become a Traitor, because it’s a hard job. There’s a lot to do, so they should want to become a Traitor. But what we always say to everyone is that once you enter the game, you could be made a Traitor at any point. As you can see at the end of Episode 1, we picked our original two Traitors, and then we left it in their hands who they were going to pick as the third one and that was Katie and Xavier.


	Cotton: You’re right, though. It’s more difficult working out who those initial Traitors should be when they’re a cast of regular people who we don’t have a history with on a reality show or on television. That then comes down to casting, and really digging into who these people are and the characters that they are. We don’t decide who the Traitors are until everyone’s arrived at the castle. So they’ve been on the train, and we’ve seen them interact. They’ve all sat down with Alan and had quite in-depth chats with him about whether they want to be a Traitor or not.
	

	
		That uncertainty extends to the cast’s hunt for Traitors as well. The celebrities often have pre-existing relationships and feuds that can guide accusations. But in this premiere, the cast is largely at a loss on who to target at the first roundtable.	

	Franks: What’s so exciting is that they all come in with a completely clean slate. It’s a game about identity, and they can basically be whoever they want. But we’re watching them get to know each other, and we’re getting to know them at the same time. So it’s a level playing field for the viewers and the players, which is really exciting to watch. You feel very much like you’re part of the process.


	
		One of the biggest differences between the celebrity and civilian editions is the impact of the money. Watching celebrities play challenges for money doesn’t quite have the same thrill because, depending on their personal wealth and situation, $250,000 may be life changing or it may be a drop in the bucket. But for the “New Blood” cast, it is different. Mark Zgoda makes a comment after the first challenge, where they add $50,000 to the prize pot: “That’s a full person’s salary already added to the pot.” This money will simply mean more for these players. How does that change the game play?	

	Rees-Jones: We love that moment, and I’m glad you mentioned it. That perfectly summarized all of their approaches to the game, to the challenges, to the missions, and yeah, the money means so much to them. As far as the game is concerned, what it means is that they all have to work together really hard to build that prize pot. But ultimately, that also means that betrayal cuts even deeper. Because the whole game is built around the Faithfuls and the Traitors coming together to put up that prize pot, which in one mission can be as much as the person’s yearly salary, then when treachery happens, it hurts even more. But to see the missions play out and to see them throw themselves into it, whatever their age or physical ability, was amazing. You see what it meant to them at the end of Episode 1 when they win a huge amount of money.


	
		Alan also reveals in the premiere that, for the first time, each Traitor banished from the castle will earn a $15,000 bonus for the prize pot. Is that in addition to the possible $250,000 they can raise?	

	Rees-Jones: It’s in addition to the $250,000. We’ve talked about it for a while. Obviously, the most important thing is to get a Traitor out. But we felt there was something really interesting in that added incentive.


	
		That could make the difference between speaking up or staying quiet at the roundtable if you know there is more money on the line.	

	Franks: Exactly!


	
		In the premiere, as soon as they arrive in the castle, you let them roam free. But after several seasons of this show, this cast has been watching at home and they clearly know the place. A few even knew which book to pull to open the secret room in the library. Does that much familiarity with the castle pose any issues?	

	Cotton: I love that they knew the castle! The castle is a real place. It’s not like it’s a “Big Brother” house that’s reconstructed every year. So I think we all love the fact they felt at home immediately in there, and that they knew the game and they knew the rhythm of it. Every year is a different murder mystery, so we put a lot of plans in place to keep the players on their toes. But we never change the core game of Traitors versus Faithfuls. It will never change the overall rhythm of the game, but we always, every season, put in new twists and turns just to keep them guessing even if they think they know it and the castle.

	Rees-Jones: I think it actually really helped this cast. To have a sense of familiarity meant they felt comfortable in their surroundings and they played hard straight away.


	
		James and Oliver Phelps are here! Fred and George Weasley from the “Harry Potter” movies are seen being mischievous in the premiere. What can you tease about their role this season?	

	Rees-Jones: That is their role! They’re mischievous, mysterious castle creepers.


	
		What a job title to have.	

	Rees-Jones: Yeah, it was just a fun tongue-in-cheek extension of the murder mystery world. You have Alan’s castle, and you would imagine in that world there would be people that are keepers of the castle. So there’s some fun to be had with little scenes that can be peppered throughout the season.

	Cotton: One of the things I’m most excited about with the NBC version is that we have a chance to expand this world to a broader audience. In the U.K., the show has become a massive shared viewing experience, like a family hit. People gather with their children to watch the show. Although it’s about betrayal and murder, there’s also elements of “Harry Potter” and magical fantasy within the show as well. So I feel like who [James and Oliver] are, and that world they’re from, sort of ties in neatly with the world of “The Traitors” too.


	
		In the first challenge, there is a decoy crate filled with salmon. Was this an acknowledgement that there is apparently not enough salmon in Scotland for your previous casts, who protested the lack of smoked salmon at breakfast before?	

	Franks: It’s always about the salmon!


	It’s hard not to make that connection given how much your last celebrities talked about it!

	Franks: Yes, we do like putting in little Easter eggs like that for the fans.
	
		In previous seasons, the music in the show has been appropriately moody but generic. “New Blood” has covers of real songs, including Justin Timberlake’s “Cry Me a River” at a particularly sinister moment. Was this something new available to you on broadcast?	

	Franks: That was one of the things we were so excited about in terms of making the show feel familiar but also fresh, that we were going to be able to use some commercial music in this version. I don’t know how you felt watching it, but I feel like there’s tonally a shift in the way that it feels and I think the commercial music definitely helps with that.
	

	
		You don’t often speak about why you chose the Traitors, but you did let them choose two accomplices to audition for the third Traitor slot. We don’t yet see who wins, but what did you think about their two choices, Katie and Xavier?	

	Cotton: I love that the Traitors chose Katie and Xavier, because they chose almost completely opposite people.


	
		The height difference alone! You can barely get them both in the same camera frame.	

	Cotton: Right! They are so different that it was surprising and really thrilling for us when it happened.


	
		Should we be worried that, physically, the book they have to steal is almost as big as Katie? Seems like it might be hard for her to sneak away with it!	

	Cotton:You’ll have to wait and see what happens!

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

title: ‘Resident Evil’ Video Game References: All the Zombies, Weapons and Easter Eggs in Zach Cregger’s Reboot

		‘Resident Evil’ Video Game References: All the Zombies, Weapons and Easter Eggs in Zach Cregger’s Reb
body:
Sep 17, 2026 5:30pm PT	
	

	
		‘Resident Evil’ Video Game References: All the Zombies, Weapons and Easter Eggs in Zach Cregger’s Reboot
	
	
			


			
			
	

									©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection
	

		
	
				

	SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “Resident Evil,” now playing in theaters.

	“Resident Evil” is one of the longest-running horror video game series, and for a time it was the highest-grossing film series based on a game (until Universal’s “Super Mario” movies dethroned them). The games started out as scary, third-person shooters that packed in scares even while the graphics were low on pixels. 

	The original Capcom game released in 1996 and introduced gamers to heroes Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine who must escape a spooky mansion filled with zombies. They later uncover the Umbrella Corporation, a pharmaceutical company that let loose a zombie virus while experimenting with bio-weapons. The 1998 sequel ramped things up and brought in Chris’ sister Claire Redfield and Leon S. Kennedy, who had to escape the zombie-infested Raccoon City. Later sequels, remakes and reboots spread the zombie virus into hillbilly homes, vampire villages and further around the world as the Umbrella Corporation’s disease took hold.

	The games have been massive hits for gamers and horror fans alike, and they were adapted into six live-action movies helmed by Paul W.S. Anderson and starring Milla Jovovich. After a failed reboot with 2021’s “Resident Evil: Welcome to Raccoon City,” the film franchise is getting revamped again by “Barbarian” and “Weapons” director Zach Cregger, who’s made a fully original story separate from the games. The movie takes place in Raccoon City and features the Umbrealla Corporation, but star Austin Abrams’ character Bryan is simply a medical courier who’s in way over his head during a not-so-routine delivery.

	Check out all of the video game references from Cregger’s movie below.


			
			
	Undead Dogs
			
								
				
	A seemingly normal dog chases Bryan when he looks for refuge in an abandoned barn after encountering his first zombie. He climbs up to the rafters for safety then foolishly chucks the ladder down at the dog, forcing him to painfully jump down to the ground to escape. But the dog keeps pursuing Bryan and rams its head through the barn wall in an attempt to bite him. When the dog gets stuck, its head opens up to reveal horrifying tendrils that snap at Bryan. In the video games, zombie dogs are one of the most classic and earliest enemies players encounter.
		
			
			
	Puker
			
								
				
	Bryan encounters a monster that spews acidic vomit at him while he’s stuck in the hospital elevator, and it’s inspired by a classic video game zombie. “Resident Evil 7: Biohazard” featured a Fat Molded that used used projectile vomit as a weapon, and many other horror games use a similarly nasty enemy type. 
		
			
			
	Revenant
			
								
				
	The Revenant is a horrifying creature in “Resident Evil Revelations 2” that’s stitched together from various bodies and parts. Sound familiar? It’s basically the same monster that chases Bryan and pulls in more living and undead bodies with its tendrils to grow larger. Bryan himself turns into a version of the monstrosity at the end of the movie.
		
			
			
	T-Virus Tendrils
			
								
				
	While it’s not named in the movie, the T-Virus is the Umbrella Corporation’s infamous experiment gone wrong. The virus spread wide and turned everyone into undead zombies with a hunger for flesh. Many of the monsters sport long tendrils that players must shoot to fully defeat them, much like in the movie.
		
			
			
	Raccoon City
			
								
				
	Raccoon City is one of the most notorious locations in the “Resident Evil” universe and the home of the shady Umbrella Corporation, which also appears in the film. Like the new movie, Umbrella has a laboratory in Raccoon City, where the zombie virus inevitably breaks out and spreads from.
		
			
			
	Umbrella Corporation
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	The Umbrella Corporation is a pharmaceutical company that secretly performed experiments with bio-organic weapons in the “Resident Evil” universe that lead to the spread of the zombie apocalypse. In the movie, Paul Walter Hauser and Zach Cherry play bumbling Umbrealla scientists trying to stop the outbreak.
		
			
			
	Locks
			
								
				
	Locked doors are a classic video game trope. They block your access to the next level, a powerful upgrade or merely prevent you from wandering too far off from your goal. Sometimes they require a key, a code or you can blast it apart with a gun and force your way through. The “Resident Evil” games have used all of these mechanics, but Bryan encounters some particularly sturdy locks in the movie.
		
			
			
	Weapons
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Weapons (no, not Cregger’s “Weapons”) obviously play a large role in killing zombies and protecting yourself in the apocalypse. Most “Resident Evil” games start out the same way as Bryan’s journey: You start out unarmed and narrowly escape the first enemy, then you find more powerful upgrades to bolster your firearm cache. Bryan picks up a handgun, shotgun and assault rifle, three classic guns from the video games.
		
			
			
	Flashlights
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	A useful tool in life and video games, “Resident Evil” flashlights illuminate dark areas but can also alert zombies to your location. Bryan uses one to make his way through the snowy wilderness, a dank sewer and Raccoon City — luckily, he doesn’t run out of batteries, like in the video games. 
		
			
			
	Looking for Ammo
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Every gamer knows the feeling of being low on ammunition as a horde of zombies creep closer. The “Resident Evil” games give you just enough bullets to scrape by, but you’ll need to search every drawer, cupboard and locked safe to find more. When Bryan finds the shotgun, he frantically explores the farmhouse for ammo as an undead woman pursues him.
		
			
			
	Stalkers
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	The “Resident Evil” series has plenty of horrifying, lumbering villains who slowly chase you throughout a level, and the movie has a similar, stitched-together monster that relentlessly trails Bryan. Nemesis, Mr. X, Lady Dimitrescu  andJack Baker are some of the video games’ scariest stalkers who follow your every foostep.
		
			
			
	First-Person POV
			
								
				
	The “Resident Evil” games started out as a third-person shooter, meaning the camera was fixed behind the player’s shoulder and followed them. Later games transitioned into first-person, which put you directly into the character’s shoes and let you see through their eyes. Cregger recreates several shots like this, where you see down the barrel of Bryan’s gun like a first-person game.

                              September 17, 2026
                            5:55 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Two fifth-grade teachers at the same Wisconsin elementary school are now convicted of sex crimes involving minors ... and somehow, the story gets even more bizarre.
      
    
            Former River Crest Elementary teacher Abigail Faust pleaded guilty Monday to child enticement and second-degree sexual assault of a child under 16. The 25-year-old admitted to sexually assaulting two 15-year-old boys -- including one whose family employed her as a nanny.
      
    
            Faust's former coworker and friend, 26-year-old Madison Bergmann, had already pleaded guilty to child enticement and sexual misconduct involving an 11-year-old student ... and was sentenced to six years in prison.
      

            And here's the wild part -- prosecutors say Faust and Bergmann were texting each other about their relationships with the boys.
      
    
            Faust had also been accused of inappropriate conduct with one of her own fifth graders, including allegedly keeping him after class and kissing him on the cheek ... but those charges were dismissed as part of her plea deal.
      
    
            She was also accused of knowing about Bergmann "making out" with the 11-year-old and failing to report it.
      
    
            Faust told the court what she did wasn't simply a mistake or bad judgment ... and said she's now in therapy trying to understand her choices.
      
    
            She's due to be sentenced in December.

            TikToker Mason Hull is fighting back against criminal charges accusing him of buying child porn online, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The 18-year-old content creator -- known for his Looksmaxxing content -- entered a not guilty plea to 15 counts of possession of child sexual abuse material.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Mason was arrested on May 5 after detectives said they found videos on his phone of children being sexually abused.
      

            According to the arrest warrant, Mason's girlfriend told cops she discovered the material when she looked through his phone because she believed he was cheating on her.
      
    
            She claimed to have found messages on the Telegram app where Mason was allegedly paying people for the videos.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            During questioning, the docs say Mason told officers he recently wanted to "try something new" and sought out taboo pornography.
      
    
            He said he spent money twice on buying videos with kids between the ages of 8 and 15. Cops say some of the videos they found showed children crying while being abused.
      
    
            As part of his release on bond, Mason was ordered not to use the internet, which prosecutors later said he violated. His lawyers told the court Mason was an influencer and said the complete bar on using the internet hindered his ability to earn a living.

body:
Lady Gaga & Michael Polansky
                          We Have a Baby Girl!!!

                September 17, 2026
                
                            11:23 AM PDT
                                                                      |

                                  September 17, 2026
                                6:06 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Lady Gaga and Michael Polansky's baby is a girl named Rose ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to the birth certificate obtained by TMZ, Rose Bean Polansky was born June 9 at 11:19 PM at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            It's unclear where the name Rose Bean originated from ... however Gaga has a large rose down her spine that she got to commemorate her performance of "La Vie En Rose" in the film "A Star is Born." The middle name Bean may have been inspired by singer/activist Carl Bean -- whom her hit "I Was Born This Way" pulled inspo from.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The baby was delivered by Dr. Robert Katz, the OB-GYN to the stars ... the same doctor who helped Ciara and Russell Wilson welcome their daughter, Sienna.
      
    
            As we reported ... Gaga was recently photographed holding her daughter close to her chest while walking with Polansky and a friend in Northern California. The couple has been spending private family time away from the spotlight.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Gaga and Polansky remain engaged and are not married ... despite a recent report claiming they had secretly tied the knot. Sources with direct knowledge told us earlier this month that close family members had seen the couple together and knew they had not gotten married.
      
    
            Gaga and Polansky got engaged in 2024. In March, Gaga said they planned to get married "soon."
